---
title: Where the list is, as state you can read
version: 1
---

**A `LazyColumn`'s scroll position is an object, `LazyListState`, and whoever holds it can read
it and move it.** `SessionList` takes one as a parameter with `rememberLazyListState()` as the
default, which is the same hoisting lesson 4 describes for any state: the list works on its own, and
a caller that needs to know where it is passes its own.

The second test in section 04's `SessionListTest` does that. It scrolls to item 14 the way a test
does, through the semantics of the node that can scroll, and prints what the state says:

```
ana@vm:~/planner$ grep -h -e 'items\|visible' app/build/test-results/testDebugUnitTest/TEST-com.example.planner.SessionListTest.xml | sed 's/.*CDATA\[//'
first visible item: 14, offset 0
items laid out: [2026-10-29, 11, 12, 2026-10-30, 13, 14, 15, 2026-10-31, 16]
total items: 40
```

Read the three lines against the code.

- **`first visible item: 14, offset 0`**. Item 14 is counted over everything the list emitted,
  headers included. Four items a day, a header and three sessions, so items 12 to 15 are Thursday:
  its header, then sessions 10, 11 and 12. Item 14 is session 11, scrolled exactly to the top.
- **`items laid out`** lists the keys of what is on screen, and the first one is
  `2026-10-29`, Thursday's header, although its index is 12 and the list starts at 14. That is the
  sticky header: pinned at the top, drawn over session 11.
- **`total items: 40`**: thirty sessions and ten headers.

```schooling-figure
{"image": "data:image/png;base64,", "alt": "The list scrolled down. The header Thursday 29 October is pinned at the top, covering a row whose text barely shows; below it SQL Databases 90 min, then the header Friday 30 October with three sessions, and the header Saturday 31 October at the bottom.", "caption": "Scrolled to item 14: Thursday's header stays pinned, drawn over session 11."}
```

The screenshot shows it. Thursday's header sits at the top, session 11 is under it, hidden but for
the descenders of its text, and session 12 below.

## Reading the state without recomposing on every pixel

`firstVisibleItemIndex` changes many times during one fling. A composable that reads it directly
recomposes on each change; one that only needs "has the list moved off the top" wants to recompose
twice, when the answer flips. `derivedStateOf` is how, and lesson 5 explains why it works:

```kotlin
val showBackToTop by remember { derivedStateOf { state.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 } }
```

Section 06 uses exactly this shape to decide when to load more sessions. Moving the list is a
suspend call on the state, `state.animateScrollToItem(0)`, run from a coroutine; lesson 11 is where
the course starts launching coroutines from the interface.
